{
    coach: { label:'For coaches', addr:'roster.coachos/coaches — members', posts:[
      { type:'post', who:AV.elena, name:'Elena S.', role:'Business coach for solo founders', time:'3d', likes:1842, cmts:167,
        txt:'10 things I wish someone had told me before I started my coaching practice:

Certification gets you confidence, not clients.
Your niche is whoever keeps saying yes.
Free sessions attract people who value free.
The website matters less than the follow-up.
Post twice a week or don’t bother.
Raise your price the day you’re fully booked.
A quiet month in marketing becomes a quiet quarter in revenue.
Testimonials beat credentials, every time.
The admin will eat you alive if you let it.
Nobody hires you for your certificate. They hire you after one conversation.

What would you add?',
        cmt:{ who:AV.tom, name:'Tom H.', txt:'“A quiet month in marketing becomes a quiet quarter in revenue” — learned that one the expensive way.' } },
      { type:'carousel', who:AV.priya, name:'Priya M.', role:'Leadership coach · ex-HR director', time:'4d', likes:2318, cmts:146,
        cap:'Saved by 900+ people last week. The five questions, one per slide →',
        bg:G.orange, slides:[
          {k:'For coaches · 5 slides', h:'The 5 questions that unstick any client', p:'Not advice. Not frameworks. Questions — the only tool that scales to every client.'},
          {k:'01', h:'“What are you pretending not to know?”', p:'Then silence. Don’t rescue them from it. The session starts when they answer.'},
          {k:'02', h:'“What would this look like if it were easy?”', p:'Strips the drama off the problem. What’s left is usually a to-do list.'},
          {k:'03', h:'“What did you do the last time this happened?”', p:'Clients forget they have a track record. Hand it back to them.'},
          {k:'04', h:'“Whose permission are you waiting for?”', p:'Nine times out of ten, the answer is “nobody’s” — said out loud, it breaks.'},
          {k:'05', h:'“What will you actually do by Friday?”', p:'A session without a Friday is a conversation. Close every loop with a date.'} ] },
      { type:'post', who:AV.priya, name:'Priya M.', role:'Leadership coach · ex-HR director', time:'5d', likes:927, cmts:58,
        txt:'Clients don’t pay for the hour.

They pay for the ten years that taught you what to say in it.

Price the decade.' },
      { type:'poll', who:AV.jonas, name:'Jonas K.', role:'Wellness & burnout coach', time:'6d', likes:432, cmts:61,
        txt:'Honest one, coaches: what actually eats your non-coaching hours? (We keep saying “admin” — let’s get specific.)',
        poll:{ meta:'1,847 votes · poll closed', opts:[
          ['Content & posting',38],['Follow-ups & lead admin',27],['Invoices & chasing payment',21],['Website & tech upkeep',14] ] } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.tom, name:'Tom H.', role:'Career transition coach', time:'1w', likes:1376, cmts:143,
        txt:'31 clients in my first year of career coaching. No audience. No ads. No funnel.

Here’s exactly what worked.

People kept asking how I’d switched careers three times without a single unemployed month. So I wrote down all 25 steps I’d used. Every one.

Then I turned the list into a self-scored checklist and gave it away. Score yourself out of 25.

Most people scored under 8.

I never had to convince anyone they needed help. The checklist did it for me.

My mistake? I charged €400 for a package that changed careers. Far too cheap. But those 31 clients became 31 referrers — and year two booked itself.' },
      { type:'post', who:AV.jonas, name:'Jonas K.', role:'Wellness & burnout coach', time:'6d', likes:684, cmts:59,
        txt:'Client: “Can we do a quick 15-minute call?”

Narrator: it was not 15 minutes.

Anyway — that’s why my booking link has buffers now. 😌' },
      { type:'teaser', who:AV.nadia, name:'Nadia R.', role:'Executive coach · 12 yrs', time:'1w',
        txt:'€19,000 in certifications before my first paying client.

Nobody tells you this at the start: the certification industry doesn’t need you to succeed. It needs you to keep enrolling.

€2,400 for the foundation. €4,800 for “practitioner.” €6,000 for “master.” Then a €5,800 business accelerator to learn to sell what the first three never taught me to sell.

That’s not education. That’s a subscription.

“You need more credentials before you can charge that.” “Clients check certifications.” “One more course and you’ll feel ready.” I believed all three. All three were wrong.

Does training matter? Of course it does — I use it weekly.

But here’s what actually got me clients:
1. Fifty coffee conversations with no agenda…' } ] },

    mentor: { label:'For mentors', addr:'roster.coachos/mentors — members', posts:[
      { type:'post', who:AV.lin, name:'Lin W.', role:'Career mentor for new grads', time:'2d', likes:1204, cmts:118,
        txt:'I cold-messaged the COO I’d admired for years. She replied in four hours.

I was two years into my career, coordinating other people’s calendars.

Full honesty about my one opening: she’d spoken at my university, and I’d taken eleven pages of notes.

So that’s what I sent. Everything I’d already applied from her talk, what happened when I did — and the three questions I still couldn’t answer.

She gave me 45 minutes. I took a day’s leave and a train across the country for it.

What that hour taught me:
1. Lead with what you’ve already done with their thinking. Not flattery — evidence.
2. Ask questions a search engine can’t answer.
3. Follow up with results, not thanks. That turned one meeting into a decade of mentorship.' },
      { type:'carousel', who:AV.aisha, name:'Aisha T.', role:'Founder mentor · 3 exits', time:'3d', likes:2054, cmts:98,
        cap:'The 12-session arc I rebuilt my mentorship around. Steal it →',
        bg:G.purple, slides:[
          {k:'For mentors · 5 slides', h:'12 sessions, one arc', p:'The structure that turned “same time next month?” into renewals asked for by session ten.'},
          {k:'Sessions 1–2', h:'Map the decision', p:'Not “what do you want to learn” — what decision do you face in the next 90 days?'},
          {k:'Sessions 3–8', h:'Work the decision', p:'Every session ends with one commitment and a date. The recap carries it forward.'},
          {k:'Sessions 9–10', h:'Prove the change', p:'Write down what moved, in the mentee’s own words. This becomes your proof — with consent.'},
          {k:'Sessions 11–12', h:'Open the next arc', p:'The renewal conversation happens before the goodbye session. Always.'},
          {k:'The rule', h:'People renew programs.', p:'They drift out of arrangements. Which one are you running?'} ] },
      { type:'post', who:AV.rob, name:'Rob F.', role:'Engineering mentor', time:'4d', likes:836, cmts:47,
        txt:'Advice is a gift.

Mentorship is a structure.

Only one of them gets renewed.' },
      { type:'poll', who:AV.lin, name:'Lin W.', role:'Career mentor for new grads', time:'6d', likes:389, cmts:44,
        txt:'Be honest, mentors — do you have a written structure for your mentorship, or is it “calls when they need me”?',
        poll:{ meta:'1,212 votes · poll closed', opts:[
          ['Written arc, sessions defined',22],['Half-structured, mostly vibes',31],['Calls whenever they ask',47] ] } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.marcus, name:'Marcus D.', role:'Product mentor · ex-VP Product', time:'6d', likes:1051, cmts:94,
        txt:'In 2011 I asked my mentor whether to take the head-of-product job.

He answered with a question: “Do you want to be paid for what you build, or for what you decide?”

Then he gave me the split I still quote: “Spend 70% of your time understanding the problem and 30% building. Juniors do the reverse.”

I interviewed. I didn’t get it — they said I needed two more years.

But the hiring manager introduced me to a founder who needed exactly my profile, and that coffee became the job that made my career.

Mentorship isn’t the wise line. It’s the chain of doors that keeps opening after the first one closes.',
        cmt:{ who:AV.aisha, name:'Aisha T.', txt:'The chain is the whole thing. My best intro came from an interview I failed.' } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.rob, name:'Rob F.', role:'Engineering mentor', time:'6d', likes:512, cmts:44,
        txt:'Mentee: “Last question, I promise.”

Also mentee: shares a doc titled “Just 3 more things (final) (v2)”

Wouldn’t trade it for anything. 😄' },
      { type:'teaser', who:AV.aisha, name:'Aisha T.', role:'Founder mentor · 3 exits', time:'1w',
        txt:'I still remember my first mentor. She changed everything.

I was 24 — sharp on paper, terrified in rooms.

She did three things nobody had done for me before. She put me in front of clients before I felt ready. She stopped me every time I ended a statement like a question. And she made me build relationships two levels above my title.

Before the biggest meeting of my life, she said five words I’ve repeated to every mentee since: “You belong at this table.”

Twenty years on, the founders I mentor tell me the same story with different names. And the data says…' } ] },

    freelancer: { label:'For freelancers', addr:'roster.coachos/freelancers — members', posts:[
      { type:'post', who:AV.marta, name:'Marta P.', role:'Copywriter · fintech', time:'2d', likes:2103, cmts:184,
        txt:'7 things I stopped doing as a freelancer that made me more money (and made me less tired):

Answering emails like I’m being graded on speed.
Giving away round three when the contract says two.
Quoting on calls instead of in writing, after a night’s sleep.
Saying “no worries!” when there were, in fact, worries.
Treating January’s drought as a personal failing instead of a pipeline fact.
Discounting for “exposure” from companies with more followers than me.
Working weekends to hit deadlines I was too polite to renegotiate.

Stopped all seven. Revenue up a third. Resentment down to zero.',
        cmt:{ who:AV.dev, name:'Dev A.', txt:'The “quoting after a night’s sleep” one paid for itself the first week I tried it.' } },
      { type:'carousel', who:AV.marta, name:'Marta P.', role:'Copywriter · fintech', time:'3d', likes:1892, cmts:121,
        cap:'Half my yeses this year came after day 8. The follow-up calendar →',
        bg:G.blue, slides:[
          {k:'For freelancers · 5 slides', h:'The follow-up calendar that closes proposals', p:'“Just checking in” is not a strategy. This is.'},
          {k:'Day 3', h:'Add something', p:'A relevant example, a case, an answer to a question they didn’t ask. Value, not pressure.'},
          {k:'Day 8', h:'Make it easier', p:'Break the scope into phases. A smaller first yes beats a stalled big one.'},
          {k:'Day 15', h:'Name a deadline — yours', p:'“I’m booking September this week” is honest scarcity. Vague availability closes nothing.'},
          {k:'Day 21', h:'Close the loop', p:'“Shall I close the file?” gets more replies than any follow-up. Nobody likes a closing door.'},
          {k:'The math', h:'Most freelancers stop at day 3.', p:'The ones who don’t, eat. Half my yeses this year came after day 8.'} ] },
      { type:'post', who:AV.dev, name:'Dev A.', role:'Brand designer · B2B SaaS', time:'4d', likes:1188, cmts:73,
        txt:'Scope creep isn’t a client problem.

It’s a silence problem.

Name it the first time, kindly, in writing — and it never becomes a pattern.' },
      { type:'poll', who:AV.sam, name:'Sam O.', role:'SEO consultant', time:'6d', likes:512, cmts:74,
        txt:'The famine starts during the feast. Proof — answer honestly: when do you follow up on a sent proposal?',
        poll:{ meta:'2,306 votes · poll closed', opts:[
          ['Day 1–3, always',18],['About a week later',24],['When I remember',41],['I don’t. They know where I am',17] ] } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.chris, name:'Chris B.', role:'Web developer · e-commerce', time:'6d', likes:1467, cmts:201,
        txt:'I tracked all 47 leads from my first year freelancing. Every enquiry. Every ghost. Every win.

I’d quit my job with zero pipeline and two months of savings.

What the spreadsheet says:
→ 11 of 47 became paying clients.
→ Referrals from old colleagues converted 4× better than cold enquiries.
→ Nearly half the losses were timing, not price — and most came back months later.
→ Every client who fought hard on price became a headache later. Every single one.

But the numbers were only half the story. The other half: the follow-up I almost didn’t send brought in my biggest client of the year. Day 12. One line.' },
      { type:'post', who:AV.chris, name:'Chris B.', role:'Web developer · e-commerce', time:'6d', likes:876, cmts:71,
        txt:'Freelance mood calendar:

Week 1: I am unstoppable.
Week 2: I am unstoppable.
Week 3: I have forgotten how to write an email.
Week 4: invoice day. I am unstoppable.' },
      { type:'teaser', who:AV.sam, name:'Yuki N.', role:'Motion designer', time:'1w',
        txt:'Time for a very honest update about my freelance business.

Three years ago this week, I posted that I was going independent. Today’s anniversary post is a different kind: I’m closing the studio.

Do I feel strange writing that? Yes. Am I sure? Also yes.

First, the honest good: the clients were wonderful, the money was the best of my career, and I grew more in three years than in the previous eight.

So why stop? Two reasons — and the first one is a character flaw.

1. I’m terrible at hard conversations. Here’s what being bad at them cost me:
→ The scope that grew 40% because I wouldn’t name it…' } ] },

    business: { label:'For small business', addr:'roster.coachos/business — members', posts:[
      { type:'post', who:AV.grace, name:'Grace T.', role:'Owner · boutique fitness studio', time:'2d', likes:1522, cmts:246,
        txt:'Hard lessons from scaling my studio to three locations as a mum of two:

1. I had to grieve the version of me who thought she could take every class, fix every rota, and repair every treadmill herself.
2. Past a certain size, someone is always unhappy with you. Choose who.
3. If people aren’t buying, you don’t have a marketing problem. You have an offer problem.
4. The customers who fight hardest on price never become regulars. Ever.
5. Hire for the job you’ll have in six months, not the one drowning you today.
6. The books don’t lie. Feelings do.
7. Protect one evening a week like a supplier contract. It is one — with your family.

What’s the hardest one you’ve learned this year?' },
      { type:'carousel', who:AV.omar, name:'Omar S.', role:'Owner · auto detailing, 2 locations', time:'4d', likes:1439, cmts:88,
        cap:'31 reviews to 240 in a year. The system, slide by slide →',
        bg:G.green, slides:[
          {k:'For owners · 5 slides', h:'The review engine', p:'Reviews are a system, not a favour. Here’s the one that took us from 31 to 240.'},
          {k:'01', h:'Ask every happy customer', p:'Not “when you remember.” Every one. The morning after, while the glow is warm.'},
          {k:'02', h:'One message, one link', p:'No “if you have a moment, maybe…” — a direct link, one sentence, signed with your name.'},
          {k:'03', h:'Reply to every review', p:'Future customers read your replies more carefully than the reviews themselves.'},
          {k:'04', h:'Put the number everywhere', p:'“240 five-star reviews” closes more than any ad we’ve run. Social proof compounds.'},
          {k:'The result', h:'“Found you on Google” became our #1 source', p:'It outran referrals in month eight. A system did that — not luck.'} ] },
      { type:'post', who:AV.omar, name:'Omar S.', role:'Owner · auto detailing, 2 locations', time:'4d', likes:964, cmts:71,
        txt:'Speed is a feature.

The first business to reply looks like the best business.

Usually becomes it, too.' },
      { type:'poll', who:AV.grace, name:'Grace T.', role:'Owner · boutique fitness studio', time:'6d', likes:398, cmts:57,
        txt:'Owners — no judgment, real numbers only. How fast does a new enquiry actually get answered at your place?',
        poll:{ meta:'1,594 votes · poll closed', opts:[
          ['Within the hour',19],['Same day',34],['Next day',29],['When we get to it',18] ] } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.hana, name:'Neha J.', role:'Owner · tutoring centre', time:'6d', likes:1108, cmts:89,
        txt:'Twelve years running this business this month. Twelve things I know for sure — the short version:

If money comes in the door, you live. If it doesn’t, you die. Everything else is commentary.

Growth isn’t one big idea. It’s ten small edges, stacked: answer first, quote same-day, invoice same-week, follow up twice, ask for the review.

Recurring revenue is heaven. Repeat customers are good. Pure project work is a treadmill with teeth.

Cheap customers are the most expensive thing you will ever buy.

And the one that took me a decade to accept: there are no business problems. Only people problems, wearing disguises.' },
      { type:'post', who:AV.grace, name:'Grace T.', role:'Owner · boutique fitness studio', time:'6d', likes:743, cmts:66,
        txt:'The four horsemen of small business:

1. “Do you do discounts?”
2. “Can you hold it till Friday?”
3. “I saw it cheaper online.”
4. “Actually, cancel.”

Still love this job. Mostly. 😅' },
      { type:'teaser', who:AV.hana, name:'Hana L.', role:'Owner · catering studio', time:'1w',
        txt:'It’s been 72 hours since this community saved my business.

On Tuesday I posted something I never thought I’d share publicly: we had six weeks of cash left. Fourteen years of work — six weeks of runway.

I hit post and felt sick. I wasn’t sure what would happen next.

Here’s what happened:
✨ 214 orders in three days — more than the previous two months combined
✨ Three corporate contracts from people who’d never heard of us on Monday
✨ The autumn collection is fully funded
✨ And the part I didn’t expect…' } ] },

    corporate: { label:'For corporate & L&D', addr:'roster.coachos/programs — members', posts:[
      { type:'post', who:AV.ingrid, name:'Ingrid B.', role:'Talent development · pharma', time:'2d', likes:876, cmts:92,
        txt:'Asking for a mentor without knowing what you need is like grocery shopping hungry, without a list.

You leave with a trolley full of impressive things and nothing that makes a meal.

We rebuilt our program’s intake around one question: “What decision are you facing in the next 90 days?”

Not “what do you want to learn.” Not “who do you admire.” A decision, with a date.

Pairs matched against a decision meet more, stall less, and finish with something to show. The mentor knows why they’re in the room. The mentee knows what done looks like.

Shopping list first. Then the store.' },
      { type:'carousel', who:AV.daniel, name:'Daniel R.', role:'People programs lead · tech', time:'4d', likes:1358, cmts:79,
        cap:'Why mentoring programs die at month 3 — and the four signals that catch it →',
        bg:G.blue, slides:[
          {k:'For programs · 5 slides', h:'Programs don’t fail. They fade.', p:'The four signals that catch the fade while it’s still fixable.'},
          {k:'Signal 01', h:'Sessions stop logging', p:'Not “satisfaction drops” — meetings simply stop happening. Track sessions, not smiles.'},
          {k:'Signal 02', h:'One side goes quiet', p:'Mentor still books, mentee stops confirming — or the reverse. The asymmetry is the tell.'},
          {k:'Signal 03', h:'Goals stop moving', p:'A pair can meet monthly and progress nothing. Meeting ≠ mentoring.'},
          {k:'Signal 04', h:'The admin becomes the bottleneck', p:'When chasing attendance is a person’s job, the program is already dying of friction.'},
          {k:'The rule', h:'Flag at week 3 of silence.', p:'Not at the year-end survey. By then you’re not fixing — you’re archaeologising.'} ] },
      { type:'post', who:AV.kwame, name:'Lucia F.', role:'HR director · manufacturing', time:'4d', likes:702, cmts:39,
        txt:'If your mentoring data feeds performance reviews, you don’t have a mentoring program.

You have a surveillance program with coffee.

Write the firewall down. Watch participation double.' },
      { type:'poll', who:AV.kwame, name:'Kwame A.', role:'OD consultant · ex-corporate L&D', time:'6d', likes:341, cmts:49,
        txt:'Program owners, honestly: how do you know your mentoring pairs are actually meeting?',
        poll:{ meta:'987 votes · poll closed', opts:[
          ['We track sessions, live',16],['Quarterly surveys',38],['We assume good faith',46] ] } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.daniel, name:'Daniel R.', role:'People programs lead · tech', time:'6d', likes:948, cmts:87,
        txt:'“What makes a good mentor?” A mentee asked me this week — and I’ve been lucky: two CEOs and one very patient plant manager mentored me.

What the best ones had in common:
1. They gave me problems slightly too big for me, then didn’t rescue me early.
2. They told me the thing nobody else would say to my face.
3. They opened doors — and then disappeared from the story so I walked through alone.
4. They kept showing up after the promotion, when there was nothing left in it for them.

We now select mentors for our program against those four. Seniority isn’t on the list.',
        cmt:{ who:AV.claire, name:'Claire V.', txt:'Number 4 is the real filter. It removes half the volunteers and keeps the right half.' } },
      { type:'post', who:AV.ingrid, name:'Ingrid B.', role:'Talent development · pharma', time:'6d', likes:428, cmts:39,
        txt:'Year-end mentoring survey:

“Did your pair meet regularly?” — 94% yes
Calendar data: 31% met after March

Anyway. That’s why we track sessions now, not vibes. 🙃' },
      { type:'teaser', who:AV.claire, name:'Claire V.', role:'Head of L&D · 1,200-person firm', time:'1w',
        txt:'It’s been 90 days since we rebuilt our mentoring program, and I owe this community an update.

In March I posted that our program was dying quietly: 214 pairs on paper, and I couldn’t tell you how many had met that month. The year-end survey said “great.” The calendars said otherwise.

I wasn’t sure publishing that was wise. Neither was my CHRO.

Here’s what 90 days of visibility changed:
✦ Active pairs: 31% → 78%
✦ Quiet pairs get flagged at week three — five saved matches last month alone
✦ The quarterly report went from a satisfaction slide to…' } ] }
  };
